pages.text: Light climbing out of gravity loses energy. Over a height H the fraction lost is $(thing)gH/c²$() - about 2.5×10⁻¹⁵ up a 22.5-metre tower. In 1959 Pound and Rebka measured it with the gamma ray of iron-57, whose line is so sharp that even this shows.

The $(item)Pound-Rebka Tower$() is built 1 to 8 storeys tall, 7.5 m each. A $(item)Cobalt-57 Source$() sits on a Doppler drive at the foot, the absorber at the top. Move the source up at exactly $(thing)v = gH/c$() - under a micrometre a second - and the climb is cancelled.

Counting decides how sure you are: the line is 190 µm/s wide, and N gamma rays find its centre to 190/√N. Count until the shift stands five times above that error, and set v within two of it. Keep the tower at the air's temperature: each kelvin between source and absorber shifts the line by 0.66 µm/s - as much as the whole effect.
